Chapter 1: The Comfort of Familiar Stories About Gender.
You know, it’s incredibly easy to fall back on familiar explanations, especially when we’re talking about the differences between men and women. Think about those moments at family gatherings, where someone cracks a joke about how men just can’t multitask, or how women have a natural touch for nurturing.
These little comments usually slip by unnoticed, almost like background noise. Why? Because they sound harmless, even a bit scientific — after all, we hear them everywhere: in the news, in classrooms, and in all those best-selling books.
But here’s something to pay attention to: beneath those casual remarks, there’s a powerful belief that men and women are simply born different — that our brains are wired in opposite ways. This idea gets repeated so often, it starts shaping how we see ourselves and each other.
It influences how we raise our kids, how teachers might treat students, and even how adults approach their careers or relationships.
The story goes that biology already decided what each of us is good at, what we’ll enjoy, and how we’ll act.
And you can see why this story is so appealing. It gives a sense of order in a world that’s often unpredictable. If boys just naturally love trucks and girls are drawn to dolls, then parents can relax, feeling like they’re just following nature’s plan. If there aren’t many women in science or leadership? Well, that’s not society’s fault — it’s just the way things are. This kind of thinking lets everyone off the hook from questioning the status quo.
But over time, cracks start to show in this tidy picture. Maybe a teacher notices a few girls excelling at math, even though they claim not to like it. Or a dad sees his son, who’s supposed to be all rough and tumble, quietly lost in drawing. Or maybe a manager looks at her team and wonders why, despite always choosing the “best person for the job,” there’s still not much diversity. These little doubts often get brushed aside, explained away by a funny story or the latest brain scan headline.
We’re surrounded by stories that reinforce the idea of hardwired gender differences. Magazines promise to unlock the secrets of “the female brain” or “the male brain,” explaining everything from shopping habits to how we talk. TV shows and movies play up these differences for laughs — or for drama. And even scientific research, with all its authority, often gets filtered through what our culture already believes.
But what if these stories are more comforting than true? What if the differences we see aren’t just about biology, but are shaped by the world around us?
So, let’s start this journey by taking a closer look at the science — and at how society shapes not just what we believe, but what we see as possible.
